## Overview

::: {.callout-important}
## Focus for Today
This lab is a **hands-on workshop** to develop your Research Plan. By the end of today, you will have:

- Operationalised your IV and DV for your chosen topic
- Written and justified your hypotheses
- Decided on your experimental design
- Matched your design to the appropriate statistical test
- Begun drafting your Method section
:::

Today's activities directly prepare you for the **Research Plan assessment** (due Week 16, Friday 27 February).

---

## Activity 1: Operationalisation Workshop (30 min)

### Choose Your Topic

The Research Plan requires you to investigate ONE of these three questions:

1. **Font difficulty → Memory**: Does reading in a harder-to-read font improve retention?
2. **Hydration → Cognitive performance**: Does drinking water improve cognitive task performance?
3. **Eye contact → Perceived trustworthiness**: Does eye contact affect how trustworthy someone seems?

::: {.callout-note}
## Your Topic
Write down which topic you've chosen (or are leaning towards) before continuing.
:::

### Understanding Operationalisation

::: {.callout-tip}
## What is Operationalisation?
Turning an abstract concept into a **concrete, measurable variable**. Your description must be specific enough that another researcher could replicate your study exactly.
:::

**1. Which of these is a well-operationalised IV?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Stress level</option><option value=''>Amount of exercise</option><option value='answer'>20 minutes of moderate cycling (heart rate 120-140 bpm) vs 20 minutes of seated rest</option><option value=''>High vs low anxiety</option></select>

**2. Which of these is a well-operationalised DV?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Memory performance</option><option value=''>How well they did on the test</option><option value='answer'>Number of words correctly recalled from a 20-word list (range: 0-20)</option><option value=''>Whether they remembered things</option></select>

### Learning from Examples

Here's how operationalisation works with topics **different from your assessment**:

**Example: Caffeine → Alertness**

> **IV**: Caffeine consumption with two levels:
>
> - Condition 1: 200mg caffeine capsule (equivalent to ~2 cups of coffee)
> - Condition 2: Placebo capsule (identical appearance, no caffeine)
>
> **DV**: Alertness measured by:
>
> - Task: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (10-minute sustained attention task)
> - Scoring: Mean reaction time to stimuli (milliseconds)
> - Range: Continuous, typically 200-500ms

Notice the specificity: exact dosage, how conditions are matched, what task, what metric.

**Example: Background Music → Concentration**

> **IV**: Audio condition with two levels:
>
> - Condition 1: Instrumental background music (60-70 dB, classical piano)
> - Condition 2: Silence (ambient noise only, <30 dB)
>
> **DV**: Concentration measured by:
>
> - Task: Proofreading task — identify spelling errors in a 500-word passage
> - Scoring: Number of errors correctly identified
> - Range: 0-15 (15 errors embedded)

### Apply to Your Topic

**3. For your chosen topic, complete this IV template:**

> "The independent variable is _____________ with two levels:
>
> **Condition 1**: _____________________________________________
>
> **Condition 2**: _____________________________________________"

**4. For your chosen topic, complete this DV template:**

> "The dependent variable is _____________ measured by:
>
> **Task/Measure**: ___________________________________________
>
> **Scoring**: _______________________________________________
>
> **Range**: ________________________________________________"

### Check Your Operationalisation

**5. The "replicability test" asks whether:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Your study is interesting enough to replicate</option><option value='answer'>Another researcher could run the exact same study from your description</option><option value=''>The results would be the same if repeated</option><option value=''>Your participants could do the task again</option></select>

::: {.callout-warning}
## Self-Check
Read your operationalisation aloud. Could a stranger run your exact study from this description alone? If not, add the missing details.
:::

## Activity 2: Hypothesis Writing Practice (25 min)

### Writing Your Null Hypothesis

The null hypothesis (H₀) states there is NO effect or NO difference.

**1. A null hypothesis predicts:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The effect you expect to find</option><option value='answer'>No difference or no effect between conditions</option><option value=''>The direction of the effect</option><option value=''>What you hope will happen</option></select>

**2. Write a null hypothesis for YOUR topic:**

H₀: _________________________________________________

### One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

**3. A one-tailed hypothesis:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Tests for any difference</option><option value='answer'>Predicts a specific direction of effect</option><option value=''>Is always more appropriate</option><option value=''>Requires no justification</option></select>

**4. A two-tailed hypothesis:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Predicts a difference without specifying direction</option><option value=''>Predicts no effect</option><option value=''>Is never appropriate in psychology</option><option value=''>Is only used for correlations</option></select>

### Making the Decision

**5. When should you use a one-tailed hypothesis?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Whenever you want more statistical power</option><option value=''>When you're not sure what will happen</option><option value='answer'>When prior research consistently supports a specific direction</option><option value=''>Always - it's better practice</option></select>

**Example justification for direction:**

> "I have chosen a **one-tailed** hypothesis predicting that caffeine will **decrease** reaction times because:
>
> - McLellan et al. (2016) meta-analysis found caffeine consistently improved reaction time across 21 studies
> - The adenosine-blocking mechanism provides theoretical basis for increased alertness
> - No studies have found caffeine impairs reaction time in healthy adults"

> "I have chosen a **two-tailed** hypothesis because:
>
> - While some studies show music improves concentration (Rauscher et al., 1993), others show it impairs performance (Perham & Vizard, 2011)
> - The effect may depend on task type, music type, and individual differences
> - I cannot confidently predict which direction the effect will go"

### Write Your Hypotheses

**Two-tailed version:**

H₁: _________________________________________________

**One-tailed version (if you can justify it):**

H₁: _________________________________________________

**Your justification:**

> "I have chosen a [one-tailed / two-tailed] hypothesis because:
>
> _________________________________________________________"

### Quick Checks

True or False: A one-tailed hypothesis gives you more statistical power to detect an effect in the predicted direction. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: If your effect goes in the opposite direction to your one-tailed prediction, you can still claim statistical significance. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

## Activity 3: Design & Analysis Matching (25 min)

### Choosing Your Design

**1. In a between-subjects design, participants:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Experience only ONE condition each</option><option value=''>Experience ALL conditions</option><option value=''>Are matched in pairs across conditions</option><option value=''>Drop out before completing the study</option></select>

**2. In a within-subjects design, participants:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Experience only one condition each</option><option value='answer'>Experience ALL conditions</option><option value=''>Are tested only once</option><option value=''>Cannot be counterbalanced</option></select>

### Evaluating Trade-offs

**3. The main advantage of between-subjects designs is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>More statistical power</option><option value=''>Fewer participants needed</option><option value='answer'>No order effects, practice effects, or carryover</option><option value=''>Simpler randomisation</option></select>

**4. The main advantage of within-subjects designs is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Each participant serves as their own control, increasing power</option><option value=''>No need for counterbalancing</option><option value=''>Participants prefer them</option><option value=''>Faster data collection</option></select>

**5. The main disadvantage of within-subjects designs is:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Less statistical power</option><option value=''>More participants needed</option><option value='answer'>Order effects, practice effects, and demand characteristics</option><option value=''>Cannot use t-tests</option></select>

### Apply to Your Topic

**6. Describe what a between-subjects version of YOUR study would look like:**

> "Group A (n = ___): _________________________________________
>
> Group B (n = ___): _________________________________________"

**7. Describe what a within-subjects version of YOUR study would look like:**

> "All participants (n = ___) would: ____________________________
>
> Order would be counterbalanced by: __________________________"

**8. For YOUR topic, identify one specific trade-off:**

> "A key consideration for my study is: _________________________
>
> This makes [between / within] subjects more appropriate because: ___"

### Matching Design to Test

**9. A between-subjects design with two groups requires:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Paired samples t-test</option><option value='answer'>Independent samples t-test</option><option value=''>One-sample t-test</option><option value=''>Correlation</option></select>

**10. A within-subjects design with two conditions requires:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Paired samples t-test</option><option value=''>Independent samples t-test</option><option value=''>One-sample t-test</option><option value=''>Chi-square test</option></select>

**11. Why does design determine the statistical test?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Statistical software requires you to specify</option><option value=''>It's a tradition in psychology</option><option value='answer'>Different designs produce different data structures that require different analyses</option><option value=''>Both tests give the same answer anyway</option></select>

### Write Your Complete Justification

> "This study will use a [between-subjects / within-subjects] design because:
>
> [Specific advantage for your topic]: _________________________
>
> [How you'll address the main disadvantage]: __________________
>
> Given this design, I will use a [independent / paired] samples t-test because [how the data structure matches the test]: _______________"

## Activity 4: Method Section Draft (30 min)

Use these templates to draft each subsection for YOUR chosen topic.

### Design Subsection

> "This study employs a [between-subjects / within-subjects] experimental design. The independent variable is _____________ with two levels: _____________ and _____________. The dependent variable is _____________ measured by _____________."

### Participants Subsection

> "[Number] participants will be recruited from [source].
>
> [For between-subjects]: Participants will be randomly assigned to either the ______ condition (n = __) or the ______ condition (n = __).
>
> [For within-subjects]: All participants will complete both conditions, with order counterbalanced."

### Materials Subsection

> "Materials include: [Be specific enough to replicate]
>
> - Stimuli: ________________________________________________
> - Measures: ______________________________________________
> - Equipment: _____________________________________________"

### Procedure Subsection

> "Participants will be tested [individually / in groups]. After providing informed consent:
>
> 1. [First step with timing]: _________________________________
> 2. [Second step]: _________________________________________
> 3. [Continue...]: __________________________________________
>
> The session will last approximately __ minutes."

---

## Peer Feedback

If time permits, exchange your draft Method with a neighbour.

**Feedback questions:**

1. Could you replicate this study from the description alone?
2. Are all variables clearly operationalised?
3. Is the design-to-test justification clear?
4. What specific details are missing?

---

## Summary

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Takeaways

**Operationalisation**

- IV: Specify EXACTLY how conditions differ
- DV: Specify EXACTLY how you'll measure the outcome

**Hypotheses**

- One-tailed: Requires justification from prior research
- Two-tailed: Safe choice when direction uncertain

**Design**

- Between-subjects → Independent t-test
- Within-subjects → Paired t-test
- Choice depends on specific trade-offs for your topic

**Method Section**

- Design: Type, IV with levels, DV with measurement
- Participants: N, recruitment, assignment
- Materials: Everything needed to replicate
- Procedure: Step-by-step what happens
:::
